methodological_rigor.justification: Small prospective clinical trial with 10 OSCC cases and 10 controls with justified sample size from pilot study. Standardized measurement procedure (30 min fasting, 20 min acclimation, 3 repeated measurements). Histopathological confirmation via biopsy for all cases. However, major limitations include very small sample size, no blinding of device operator, narrow lesion types (8 tongue, 2 lip only, no floor of mouth/palate/gingiva despite claiming these as high-risk), single-center, no control for potential confounders beyond exclusion criteria.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Diagnostic accuracy study investigating novel non-invasive intraoral infrared thermometry for OSCC detection. Potential clinical utility for early detection and point-of-care screening, but evidence is highly preliminary with insufficient sample size to establish clinical applicability. Perfect sensitivity/specificity reported (1.0) on tiny sample is not credible for clinical practice without validation.

reporting_quality.justification: Methods adequately describe device specifications (Melexis MLX90614 sensor, 0.02°C resolution, 0.3°C accuracy) and standardization procedures. Results section lacks comprehensive diagnostic accuracy reporting (no 95% CIs for sensitivity/specificity, no mention of likelihood ratios). No adherence to STARD checklist for diagnostic accuracy studies. Discussion appropriately addresses limitations but findings are overinterpreted given sample size. No data availability statement provided.

novelty_literature.justification: First application of custom-designed intraoral IR sensor for OSCC detection, filling methodological gap in thermal imaging approaches which previously used external facial thermography or DITI. Device innovation is genuine. However, principle of thermal detection for cancer diagnosis well-established; contribution is primarily engineering-based rather than discovery-based. Limited evidence of clinical utility at this stage.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with contextual epidemiologic introduction and clear methods describing device and measurement protocol. Results presented accurately if simply. Discussion appropriately cites prior thermography literature. However, significant overstatement of findings given sample size—claiming sensitivity/specificity of 1.0 on 10 cases is not credible. Discussion somewhat optimistic tone given preliminary nature; limitations section appropriately identifies small sample size as primary concern.

key_strengths: Novel custom-designed intraoral infrared sensor representing genuine engineering innovation over prior external thermography approaches for oral cancer detection
Careful standardization of measurement conditions (30 min fasting, 20 min acclimation, ambient temperature controlled) and triple-measurement averaging to minimize error
Prospective design with histopathological confirmation of all cases via biopsy and justified sample size from prior pilot study
Clear description of device specifications (0.02°C resolution, 0.3°C accuracy) with portable, battery-powered design suitable for clinical use
key_concerns: Critically small sample size (10 cases, 10 controls) results in unreliable estimates of diagnostic accuracy; reported sensitivity/specificity of 1.0 with 95% CIs likely spanning 0.5-1.0, undermining clinical credibility
Narrow lesion distribution (8 tongue, 2 lip only) despite introduction emphasizing floor of mouth, palate, gingiva as high-risk sites; limits generalizability to oral cavity breadth
Lack of operator blinding and no independent reader validation of thermal measurements; potential for bias in measurement interpretation
No validation in independent cohort or prospective setting; diagnostic performance claimed on same population used for threshold determination (overfitting risk)
chief_reviewer.rationale: Preliminary device study with genuine innovation but severely underpowered. Small sample, lack of blinding, and overstatement of diagnostic accuracy (1.0 sensitivity/specificity) are major concerns. Suitable for Tier 4 specialized journals (e.g., device/methods journals, dental technology) with major revisions: larger sample, independent validation, formal reporting of confidence intervals, and appropriately tempered conclusions pending multi-center validation.
